paras: The lynching of Wm. Smeal was the hanging of a Black farm worker by a mob near the Jefferson and Lawrenceville road in Gwinnett County, Georgia, in mid-February 1882. Accused of stealing a horse, Smeal was taken from his cabin at night, whipped until he confessed, and hanged from a black-jack tree, where his body was found the next day. A short Athens dispatch carried the story nationally, and the local Jefferson Herald, while calling horse stealing a grave offense, condemned the killing as lynch law.

Smeal worked on the plantation of Thomas (Tom) Dillard, whom one dispatch called "a prominent planter," and lived in a cabin there. The same dispatch described him as "an industrious man, with a bad reputation, however, as a thief." According to both the Jefferson Herald and the Athens dispatch, a horse had been stolen in the neighborhood during the preceding week and suspicion fell on Smeal.

A group of men, "a body of men" in the Herald's words and a "mob" in the wire reports, organized themselves and went at night to Dillard's place, where they broke open the cabin and carried Smeal out. They whipped him, taking turns at the beating in one account, until he confessed to the theft and led them to where the horse was tied in the woods. The men then put a trace chain, taken from a wagon according to the Indiana State Sentinel's version, around his neck and hanged him from the limb of a black-jack tree near the Jefferson and Lawrenceville road. The Herald placed the spot "just over in the edge of Gwinnett county," where the body was found hanging.

The Athens dispatch reported "much indignation" over the killing and said the perpetrators would be made to answer to the law if they could be discovered. The Herald likewise wrote that the participants had made themselves liable. No report of an inquest, arrest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

Most readers learned of the killing through a brief telegraphic dispatch datelined Athens, February 14, which ran the next day in the St. Paul Daily Globe, the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer and the Sacramento Daily Record-Union. The same day it appeared in the Salt Lake Herald, the Memphis Daily Appeal, the Los Angeles Herald and, cut to two lines, the Rock Island Argus. Headlines included "Negro Horse-Thief Lynched," "Horse Thief Hanged by a Mob" and "Summary Punishment," and the Wheeling paper added the subhead "Justice as Dealt Out in Georgia." The telegraph garbled the county as "Gurney," "Guernsey" and "Guerncie," and the Memphis paper printed the victim's name as "Smear" and the plantation as "Bullard's."

In the following ten days the story shrank to digest lines: the South Kentuckian of Hopkinsville listed "Wm. Smeal, col." as hung by a mob at Athens "for horse-stealing," and the Mower County Transcript and the Superior Times reported that "a negro horse-thief" had been lynched in "Gurney County, Ga., on the 14th." Another brief, carried by the Iola Register and the Grenada Sentinel, said a mob had visited Smeal "the other night" and whipped him until he "acknowledged horsestealing."

The longer Athens dispatch, printed a week later in the Indiana State Sentinel under "Hanged for Theft," called it "one of the most extraordinary lynchings on record," described Smeal as a "poor wretch" whose "only crime was that of stealing horses," and called the hanging an "atrocious act." The Jefferson Herald, quoted in the Savannah Morning News's roundup of Georgia papers, said it could not vouch for the account it had obtained and that "no punishment is too severe" for a horse thief, but held that punishing a man without trial was wrong because "lynch law is as dangerous to a community as a horse thief."

The accounts differ on the date: the short wire dated February 14 said the mob came "last night" and the body was found that day, while the longer Athens dispatch put the mob's visit on Sunday night and the discovery on "yesterday morning." The Herald said only that the body was found "last Monday," and the later digests gave the date as the 14th.

accounts.label: Athens dispatch (long)
accounts.gist: Men organized on Sunday night, took turns beating Smeal until he confessed, hanged him with a trace chain from a wagon to a black-jack tree; found 'yesterday morning'; much indignation, perpetrators to be prosecuted if found.

accounts.label: Jefferson Herald (local weekly)
accounts.gist: A negro was found 'last Monday' hanged with a trace chain just inside Gwinnett county; the paper gave the whipping-and-confession account but said it could not vouch for it, and condemned lynch law.

framing.detail: The Jefferson Herald said 'no punishment is too severe' for a horse thief but that punishment without trial was wrong and the lynchers were liable.
The long Athens dispatch called it 'one of the most extraordinary lynchings on record' and an 'atrocious act', and Smeal a 'poor wretch'.
Most papers ran the short wire under 'Negro Horse-Thief Lynched' or 'Horse Thief Hanged by a Mob'; Wheeling added 'Justice as Dealt Out in Georgia'.
Digests reduced it to a line about a 'negro horse-thief' lynched for horse-stealing.

versions.value: Mob on Sunday night (Feb. 12); body found 'yesterday morning' (Feb. 13 by the Feb. 14 dateline)

record_check.dossier: One victim, Smeal ('Wm. Smeal'); 'Vim Smeal' is an OCR variant and Thomas Dillard was the plantation owner, not a victim.
Athens is only the wire dateline; the hanging was near the Jefferson and Lawrenceville road in the edge of Gwinnett County.
'Guernsey' is a wire garble; the local Herald places it in Gwinnett County. The body was found the next morning (Feb. 13 per the long dispatch, Feb. 14 per the short wire).
Mob on the night of Feb. 12 (long dispatch) or Feb. 13 (short wire); 1882-02-13 is acceptable but the night of Feb. 12-13 is the more detailed version.
